entities.name: Richard Wagner
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard Wagner (1813–1883) was a German composer, conductor, and polemicist who revolutionised opera through his concept of the Gesamtkunstwerk—the 'total work of art' unifying music, drama, poetry, and visual spectacle. His influence on Western music is rivalled only by Bach and Beethoven.

Wagner's mature operas—'Tristan und Isolde' (1865), 'Die Meisteringer von Nürnberg' (1868), and the four-opera cycle 'Der Ring des Nibelungen' (1876)—shattered conventional tonality and dramatic structure. 'Tristan' introduced chromatic harmonies so radical that they pointed directly toward the dissolution of tonal music in the 20th century.

To stage his vision, Wagner designed and built the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, a purpose-built opera house with a hidden orchestra pit that opened in 1876 for the first complete 'Ring' cycle. The Bayreuth Festival continues annually to this day.

Wagner's anti-Semitic writings and his posthumous adoption by the Nazi regime remain deeply controversial. Yet his musical innovations—the leitmotif system, through-composed opera, and expanded orchestral palette—reshaped film scoring, symphonic music, and theatrical practice worldwide.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Wagner's innovations in opera transformed Western music, influencing generations of composers and shaping the development of modern drama. His radical harmonies and dramatic structures paved the way for 20th-century musical experimentation.
